name: Wat Benchamabophit
significance: Commissioned by King Chulalongkorn in 1899 next to his new Dusit Palace and finished in 1911, this royal monastery was designed by Prince Narisara Nuwattiwong and faced in imported Carrara marble, giving it its popular name, the Marble Temple. Its cruciform ordination hall holds a Sukhothai-style principal Buddha cast from melted brass cannon, beneath which the king's ashes are interred, and a surrounding gallery displays 52 Buddha images in differing postures.

name: Erawan Shrine
significance: A public shrine in central Bangkok housing a four-faced image of Phra Phrom, the Thai form of Brahma, which the Fine Arts Department designed and enshrined on 9 November 1956 for the state-owned Erawan Hotel. It has remained one of the city's busiest devotional sites even after the original hotel was demolished in 1987 and replaced by the Grand Hyatt Erawan, and it is a much-cited example of Hindu, Buddhist and Thai animist worship converging at one altar.
story: The shrine is said to have been raised to offset the bad karma of laying the hotel's foundation on an inauspicious date, after which the accidents and delays that had plagued the building work reportedly stopped.

name: Sri Maha Mariamman Temple, Bangkok
significance: Founded in 1879 by the Tamil migrant Vaithi Padayatchi, this Silom temple is the oldest and most important Hindu shrine in Thailand, serving the Tamil community that settled in Bangkok as gem traders and cattle keepers from the late 1850s onward. A six-metre gopura carved with deity figures fronts the complex, and a gilded copper dome covers the main sanctum, with subsidiary shrines to Ganesha, Murugan, Shiva, Vishnu, Lakshmi, Kali, Saraswati and Nataraja.

name: Wat Rong Khun (White Temple)
significance: The original temple here had fallen into disrepair by the end of the twentieth century, and the Chiang Rai national artist Chalermchai Kositpipat rebuilt it entirely at his own expense as an offering to the Buddha, opening it to visitors in 1997 and funding it with more than 40 million baht of his own money. Its all-white, mirror-inlaid buildings are laid out as a walk-through allegory, with a bridge over a pit of reaching hands standing for the passage beyond desire; work is projected to continue until about 2070, and an engineering survey confirmed the structure sound after a 2014 earthquake.

name: Wat Phra That Lampang Luang
significance: A walled hilltop monastery founded in the fifteenth century and reckoned among the most authentic surviving examples of Lanna architecture in northern Thailand, enshrining relics said to include a hair of the Buddha and ashes from his forehead and neck. In 1732 Phraya Chaisongkhram launched his surprise attack on the Burmese garrison occupying Lampang from inside the compound, killing their commander and founding the Chet Ton dynasty; bullet damage from the fight is still shown to visitors.
story: Local tradition holds that the Buddha passed this way, accepted honey offered in a bamboo tube by Lawa people, foretold that the place would become the city of Lampakappa Nakhon, and left a hair relic that devotees believe lies beneath the central chedi.

name: Wat Phra That Hariphunchai
significance: The chief Theravada monastery of Lamphun, whose stupa is traced to about 897 in the Hariphunchai kingdom and whose present compound was founded by King Athitayarat in 1044. King Tilokaraja of Lanna rebuilt much of it in 1443 and the monk Khru Ba Sriwichai led further restoration in the 1930s; the 46-metre Chedi Suwanna, a fifteenth-century Buddha image, a nineteenth-century library and a bronze gong of 1860 stand within the walls.
story: A stone in the south-western corner of the compound bears four footprint impressions that worshippers take as proof of a visit by the Buddha.

name: Prasat Muang Tam
significance: A tenth-century Khmer sanctuary in Prakhon Chai district dedicated principally to Shiva, with Vishnu also worshipped there. Unusually for a Khmer temple it is flat rather than pyramidal, its concentric enclosures separated by L-shaped ponds; kala carvings on the lintels supply much of the dating evidence, some outer gopura lintels were left unfinished, and all the towers except the central one have been restored.

name: Sdok Kok Thom
significance: A red sandstone and laterite temple in Sa Kaeo province built under Udayadityavarman II, important less for its scale than for its stele, inscription K.235 of 1053, which records nine generations of a priestly family serving Khmer kings as royal chaplains and is a primary source for Angkorian dynastic history. The stele was taken to the national museum in Bangkok in the 1920s and damaged by fire in 1960; the site itself served as a refugee camp after 1978 before restoration began in the 1990s.
story: The inscription describes a brahmin named Hiranyadaman being summoned by the king to perform a rite that would make it impossible for the land of the Kambuja to owe allegiance to Java.

name: Wat Xieng Thong
significance: Built by King Setthathirath of Lan Xang on the tip of the Luang Prabang peninsula between the Mekong and the Nam Khan, this monastery served as a royal sanctuary until 1975, hosting coronations, festivals, relic veneration and a manuscript library. It escaped the sacking of the city in 1887 because the Black Flag commander had trained there as a monk and used it as his headquarters; the Tripitaka library was added in 1880 and the drum tower in 1961.

name: Wat Si Saket
significance: Ordered by King Anouvong in 1818, this monastery is probably the oldest structure still standing in Vientiane, its cloister walls lined with more than two thousand ceramic and silver Buddha images beneath an ornate five-tiered roof. It may have survived the destruction that followed Anouvong's revolt of 1827 precisely because Siamese forces took it over as their headquarters; the French administration restored it in 1924 and 1930, and part of it now serves as a museum.

name: Preah Khan
significance: Founded by Jayavarman VII on the ground where he defeated the invading Cham in 1181 and completed in 1191, Preah Khan was named Nagara Jayasri, the holy city of victory, and its central image of Avalokiteshvara portrayed the king's father. Flat in plan, with concentric rectangular galleries around the Buddhist sanctuary and Hindu satellite shrines, it functioned as a city, monastery and university said to have supported nearly a hundred thousand attendants before royal patronage lapsed after the fifteenth century; it was cleared in 1927–1932 and has been conserved by the World Monuments Fund since 1991.

name: Neak Pean
significance: An artificial island shrine set in the Jayatataka baray beside Preah Khan, built under Jayavarman VII and counted among the hospitals of his reign: bathers were understood to have the elements within them rebalanced and their disease cured. Four linked pools stand for water, earth, fire and wind, each with its own spout in the form of an elephant, bull, horse or lion, and the Chinese envoy Zhou Daguan recorded the site during his visit to Angkor in the late thirteenth century.
story: The pools are held to represent Anavatapta, a mythical Himalayan lake whose waters cure every illness, and the surviving horse figure is Balaha, the form Avalokiteshvara took to carry shipwrecked sailors away from the ogresses of Tamradvipa.

name: Pre Rup
significance: The state temple of King Rajendravarman, dedicated in 961 or early 962 and built as a temple-mountain of brick, laterite and sandstone south of the East Baray on an axis with the East Mebon. Two enclosure walls surround an outer platform of about 117 by 127 metres, from which a three-tiered pyramid rises to a summit carrying five towers in quincunx, the central one holding the main sanctuary and the corner towers once housing images of Lakshmi, Uma and Vishnu.
story: Its modern name means to turn the body, from a widespread Cambodian belief that funerals were held here and the ashes ritually rotated to face each direction in turn as the rite proceeded.

name: East Mebon
significance: Dedicated in 953 by King Rajendravarman to Shiva and to the memory of his parents, this temple stands on what was an island at the centre of the East Baray, now a dry reservoir. Built of sandstone, brick, laterite and stucco with two enclosing walls and three tiers, it carries a central tower flanked by four corner towers, free-standing stone elephants at the terrace corners, and four landing stages at its base showing that it was once reached by boat.

name: Phnom Bakheng
significance: Raised between 889 and 910 by Yasovarman I as the state temple of Yasodharapura, the capital he founded after moving the court from Hariharalaya, this hilltop temple-mountain predates Angkor Wat by two centuries. A moat ringed the hill and avenues ran out from it in the cardinal directions; its seven levels were read as the seven heavens, its 108 towers as lunar cycles and the 33 towers visible from the centre as the gods of Mount Meru, which the whole structure represents. Monumental Buddha sculpture was added when the site later passed to Buddhist use, and the World Monuments Fund has worked on its conservation since 2004.

name: Ta Som
deity: Dharanindravarman II, deified father of Jayavarman VII
significance: A small Bayon-style temple north-east of Angkor Thom, built at the close of the twelfth century by Jayavarman VII and dedicated to his father Dharanindravarman II, who ruled from 1150 to 1160. Its gopuras carry the four-faced towers characteristic of the style; the site was left largely unrestored until the World Monuments Fund began stabilisation in 1998, and by 2007 clearance and documentation had opened access from all four sides and allowed damaged sandstone to be reset. A strangler fig grown down through the blocks of the eastern outer gopura is its best-known feature.

name: Banteay Kdei
significance: A Buddhist monastic complex laid out under Jayavarman VII over the remains of a tenth-century temple, similar in plan to Ta Prohm and Preah Khan but smaller and simpler. Monks lived here until the 1960s; poor-quality sandstone and faulty construction left it badly decayed, Henri Marchal began conservation in 1920, and excavations by Sophia University between 1992 and 2002 recovered 274 fragments of buried Buddhist sandstone statuary.

name: Bakong
significance: Completed in 881 under Indravarman I as the state temple of Hariharalaya, the capital now called Roluos, Bakong is the earliest sandstone temple-mountain the Khmer built and the model for the pyramids that followed at Angkor. Its five-tiered central pyramid measures roughly 65 by 67 metres at the base and once held a linga at the summit; the present central tower is a twelfth-century replacement reflecting later religious change, and the pyramid was restored in the 1930s by the French conservator Maurice Glaize.
story: The plan is read as a model of the cosmos, its moats standing for the mythical oceans and its enclosing walls and terraces for the mountain ranges that ring Mount Meru.

name: Preah Ko
significance: Built in 879 by Indravarman I soon after his accession, Preah Ko sets six brick towers in two rows on a single sandstone platform, its sanctuaries honouring three deified male ancestors and their wives in association with Shiva; the front central tower commemorates Jayavarman II, who founded the Khmer empire in 802. The towers were restored in the early 1990s with German government funding.

name: Beng Mealea
significance: A large sandstone temple some 40 kilometres east of the main Angkor group whose written history is lost; it is placed in the reign of Suryavarman II purely on the strength of an architectural style identical to Angkor Wat. Three enclosing galleries with cruciform cloisters and seven-headed naga balustrades surround the central sanctuary, and the temple stood at the heart of a town ringed by a moat about 1,025 by 875 metres and 45 metres wide. It remains largely unrestored and heavily overgrown, though its carvings include the Churning of the Ocean of Milk and other Vaishnava scenes alongside some Buddhist motifs.

name: Banteay Chhmar
significance: One of the largest and most remote foundations of Jayavarman VII's great building programme, flourishing in the twelfth and thirteenth centuries in what is now Banteay Meanchey province. Its carvings include multi-armed dancing Heruka figures and other tantric imagery alongside Lokeshvara, and the settlement around it, with its moats and water channels, notably lacks the formal grid that ordered most Angkorian centres. The site is on UNESCO's tentative list and has suffered heavy looting in recent decades.

name: Prasat Thom, Koh Ker
significance: The principal temple of Koh Ker, the capital Jayavarman IV held while the Khmer court was away from Angkor, with inscriptions recording the consecration in 921 of a Shiva-linga worshipped as Tribhuvaneshvara, lord of the threefold world. Parts including the moat and inner enclosure appear to predate 921 and were absorbed into the expansion under Jayavarman IV. Two walls, brick within and laterite without at 66 by 55 metres, enclose a court holding the sanctuary, two libraries, nine linga towers in two rows and twelve smaller prasats grouped in threes, all in the sharply distinct Koh Ker style.

name: Phnom Chisor
significance: An eleventh-century Angkorian foundation of Suryavarman I crowning a 133-metre hill in Takeo province, dedicated to Shiva and in part to Vishnu, and reached by a stair of roughly 610 steps. Six brick shrines make up the complex, the central one about 60 by 50 metres within two galleries, with sandstone construction extending some 400 metres across the summit. It was repaired in 1917 under French Indochina, wrecked during the fighting of the 1970s and rebuilt in 1979, and is now visited by Buddhist and Hindu pilgrims alike.

name: Wat Phnom
significance: The Theravada temple on the artificial hill from which Phnom Penh takes its name, traditionally founded in 1372 by the woman known as Lady Penh and rebuilt repeatedly through the nineteenth century and again in 1926. King Ponhea Yat moved the Cambodian capital here in 1397 and a large stupa was later raised for him at the summit; the hill and sanctuary together stand 46 metres high, and the shrine holds four Buddha images and one of Vishnu.
story: Lady Penh is said to have gone down to the river in the rain to bathe and found a floating koki tree carrying five statues, which she housed in a shrine built on a mound raised for the purpose.

name: Po Klong Garai
deity: Shiva (mukhalinga venerated as King Po Klaung Garai)
significance: A hilltop Cham brick group above Phan Rang raised toward the end of the thirteenth century under Jaya Simhavarman III, though earlier steles, including one of 1050 commemorating a Cham victory over Panduranga, suggest it replaced or enlarged older structures. Three brick towers survive, a three-storeyed main tower, a smaller gate tower and a long saddle-roofed building, and the sanctum holds a sixteenth- or seventeenth-century mukhalinga that Cham worshippers treat as an image of the king himself. The site remains in active use for Cham festivals.
story: Po Klong Garai, whose name means great water-dragon sovereign, is remembered as a cowherd who rose to the throne, ruled wisely, turned back a Khmer invasion by winning a tower-building contest, and became a protective deity after his death.

name: Thien Mu Pagoda
deity: Maitreya Buddha, with Manjushri and Samantabhadra
significance: Founded in 1601 on the order of Nguyen Hoang, governor of Thuan Hoa, on a hill above the Perfume River, and enlarged by successive Nguyen rulers in 1665, 1695–96 and 1714. Its cult absorbed an earlier Cham goddess, Po Nagar, under the name Thien Mu, the Celestial Lady; the seven-storeyed octagonal brick tower Phuoc Duyen rises 21 metres over the site. A cyclone wrecked much of it in 1904 and rebuilding began in 1907, and in 1963 it became a centre of Buddhist protest against the Diem government.
story: An old woman in red and blue is said to have appeared on the hill, foretold that a lord would come and raise a pagoda there, and then vanished.

name: One Pillar Pagoda
significance: Built in 1049 by Emperor Ly Thai Tong and refined in 1105 under Ly Nhan Tong, this small hexagonal shrine to Avalokiteshvara stands on a single stone pillar 1.25 metres across and 4 metres high, shaped so that the whole rises like a lotus, the Buddhist emblem of purity. Destroyed in 1954, it was rebuilt the following year by North Vietnam's Ministry of Culture; a replica was raised near Saigon in the late 1950s.
story: The emperor is said to have dreamed of Avalokiteshvara seated on a lotus handing him a son; a son was born after he married a peasant girl, and he built the lotus-shaped shrine in thanks.

name: Perfume Pagoda
significance: A scattered complex of shrines and cave sanctuaries in the limestone Huong Tich hills south-west of Hanoi, with a temple recorded here in the reign of Le Thanh Tong in the fifteenth century and a stele documenting the terraces and shrines built in 1686 under Le Hy Tong. Bronze images were cast in 1767 and replaced in 1793; buildings damaged in the French and American wars were repaired, the bell tower in 1986 and the gateway in 1994. It draws one of the largest pilgrim festivals in northern Vietnam.
story: The bodhisattva Quan Am is said to have travelled south and settled at Huong Tich in order to save human souls, and a stone at nearby Phat Tich is held to preserve her footprint.

name: Bai Dinh Temple
significance: A vast Buddhist complex in Gia Vien district combining an older mountainside temple with a new 700-hectare precinct built between 2003 and 2010, among the largest in Vietnam. Its halls follow traditional Vietnamese forms, with corner eaves curving up like a phoenix tail, the Tam The hall rising 34 metres; stone, timber and tiles were sourced locally and the fittings made by regional craft villages. Mountain spirits are venerated at the site alongside the Buddhas.

name: Mariamman Temple, Ho Chi Minh City
significance: Built in the late nineteenth century by Nagarathar merchants from Tamil Nadu, with Palaniappa Chettiar named as its founder, this is the principal Hindu temple of Ho Chi Minh City. A raja-gopuram about 12 metres high fronts a mandapam, and deity figures line the outer walls. It now serves some fifty Tamil families, but most of those who come to worship are Vietnamese or Sino-Vietnamese devotees of Mariamman.

name: Candi Sewu
builtDisplay: c. 792 (Rakai Panangkaran, completed under King Indra)
significance: The second-largest Buddhist temple compound in Indonesia, named Manjusrigrha, the house of Manjushri, in an inscription of about 792; work began under Rakai Panangkaran and was completed under King Indra. Its 249 shrines are set out as a mandala representing the universe, and it was the kingdom's chief Buddhist sanctuary before Borobudur and Prambanan rose nearby. Volcanic debris buried the site, which was rediscovered early in the nineteenth century, looted during the Java War, photographed by 1867 and systematically reconstructed from 1908.
story: Local folklore held that the temples were raised in a single night by a host of demons commanded by Bandung Bondowoso, part of the Loro Jonggrang legend attached to nearby Prambanan.

name: Candi Plaosan
significance: A Buddhist compound of the mid-ninth century, dated by inscriptions to between 825 and 850 and attributed to Sri Kahulunnan, or Pramodhawardhani, daughter of Samaratungga of the Sailendra line. It comprises 174 structures, 116 stupas and 58 shrines, in two groups, Plaosan Lor to the north and Plaosan Kidul to the south, originally a single complex now divided by a road. The 2006 Java earthquake caused damage, and the excavations that followed recovered significant finds.

name: Candi Kalasan
significance: Dated by its own inscription to 778, Kalasan was raised as the Tarabhavanam, a holy building for the goddess Tara, together with a monastery, after a Sailendra preceptor persuaded Maharaja Panangkaran to found it. The shrine is cross-shaped, a twelve-cornered polygon with octagonal roof stages, and is among the oldest Buddhist candi on the Prambanan plain; despite Dutch-era repairs it is now in poor condition and less well kept than its famous neighbours.

name: Candi Mendut
significance: The oldest of the three aligned temples that include Pawon and Borobudur, built early in the ninth century under King Indra of the Sailendra dynasty; the Karangtengah inscription of 824 mentions the founding of a sacred building called the bamboo forest, generally identified with it. Its chamber holds three large stone images, the Dhyani Buddha Vairocana flanked by Avalokiteshvara and Vajrapani. Found in ruins in 1836, it was restored between 1897 and 1925 and inscribed with the Borobudur Temple Compounds as a World Heritage Site in 1991; women still pray before its relief of Hariti, protector of children, when hoping for a child.

name: Candi Pawon
significance: A small ninth-century Sailendra shrine standing on the straight line that joins Borobudur and Mendut, credited to the architect Gunadharma and admired for the simplicity, symmetry and balance that mark Central Javanese work against the later East Javanese manner. Its name derives from a Javanese word for kitchen, from a root meaning dust, and it may have served as a mortuary temple for a king; bodhisattva and tara reliefs adorn its walls. Restored in 1835 under Raffles, it was inscribed with the Borobudur Temple Compounds as a World Heritage Site in 1991.

name: Candi Sukuh
deity: Shiva, represented by a lingga, with fertility and ancestor symbolism
significance: Built about 1437, a date given as a chronogram on its western gate, this temple on the slopes of Mount Lawu takes the form of a truncated stepped pyramid on three terraces, a trapezoidal plan unlike anything else among Java's classical monuments. Its carving is openly concerned with fertility, sexuality and ancestor worship, and the temple departs from the Wastu Vidya canon because it was raised as Hindu practice on Java was already weakening. It belongs to the last phase of temple building before the island's courts turned to Islam in the sixteenth century; when Raffles visited in 1815 he found the statues damaged and the great lingga broken.

name: Candi Cetho
significance: A terraced fifteenth-century Javanese-Hindu temple at 1,495 metres on the western slope of Mount Lawu, on the boundary between Central and East Java, and one of a small group built on these slopes in the same period. Like nearby Sukuh it departs sharply from the Indian-derived forms of the eighth to tenth centuries, and it belongs to the last significant phase of temple building in Java before the island's courts converted to Islam in the sixteenth century.

name: Gedong Songo
significance: Nine small Shaiva shrines arranged in five groups along 1,270 metres of hillside near Mount Ungaran, dating to the eighth or ninth century in the early Mataram period of Central Java, with scholars variously placing them around 780 to 830 or later in the ninth century. All are dedicated to Shiva and Parvati, the third group pairing a Shiva temple with Nandi and Parvati shrines, and all follow a square sanctum plan with cube-shaped cellas and multi-storeyed superstructures. Dutch archaeologists found the site badly ruined in the nineteenth century; inscriptions of 1382, 1449 and 1452 show later activity, and much restoration has been done in recent decades.

name: Candi Penataran
significance: The largest Hindu temple complex in East Java, about 12 kilometres north-east of Blitar, built up between the twelfth and fifteenth centuries with work starting in 1197 in the Kediri era and continuing through the Majapahit period. Its main temple is dedicated to Shiva, while its reliefs range widely over Vaishnava material, particularly Rama and Krishna narratives, and its three successive courtyards anticipate the arrangement of Balinese puras. It is named in the Nagarakretagama, and King Hayam Wuruk is recorded as having made it his favourite sanctuary.

name: Candi Singhasari
significance: A thirteenth-century syncretic Hindu-Buddhist temple raised as the funerary monument of Kertanagara, last king of the Singhasari dynasty, who ruled from 1268 to 1292; a large original image of Shiva as Bhatara Guru stands in the lower southern chamber and a second cella above carries the Buddhist dedication. It is named in the Nagarakretagama and in the Gajah Mada inscription of 1351, and was never finished, as the incomplete kala head over the lower entrance shows. King Chulalongkorn of Siam visited in 1896 and took away a four-armed Ganesha now in the Bangkok National Museum.

name: Candi Jago
deity: King Vishnuvardhana, deified as Shiva in the form of Avalokiteshvara
significance: A thirteenth-century Hindu-Buddhist temple of the Singhasari kingdom about 22 kilometres from Malang, commemorating King Vishnuvardhana deified as Shiva in the form of the bodhisattva Avalokiteshvara; the name Adityawarman appears on a Manjushri image of 1343 found here. The Nagarakretagama of the fourteenth century calls it majestic and records a visit by King Hayam Wuruk on royal progress. Its bas-reliefs run through four narrative cycles, read anticlockwise in the prasawya manner.
story: Among the reliefs are scenes of King Angling Dharma, remembered as able to understand the speech of animals, alongside Tantri fables that teach moral lessons through animal characters.

name: Tirta Empul
significance: A Balinese Hindu water temple near Tampaksiring founded about 962 under the Warmadewa dynasty and dedicated to Vishnu, built around a sacred spring that is the source of the Pakerisan river. The precinct divides into three sections, with purification pools fed by some thirty spouts where pilgrims still perform the melukat bathing rite. A villa was built on the hill overlooking the temple for President Sukarno's visit in 1954.

name: Goa Gajah
significance: The Elephant Cave near Ubud, a rock-cut meditation sanctuary usually dated to the ninth century, though on stylistic grounds the shrine itself may belong to the eleventh-century Bali Kingdom. Lingam and yoni and an image of Ganesha stand within the cave, while stupas and chattra carved nearby show Buddhist use alongside the Shaiva. Dutch archaeologists rediscovered the site in 1923 and the bathing pool and its fountain figures were uncovered in 1954; the place is mentioned in a Javanese poem of 1365.
story: One local account holds that the cave was gouged out by the fingernail of the legendary giant Kebo Iwa.

name: Gunung Kawi
deity: Rock-cut memorial shrines to King Anak Wungsu and his queens
significance: An eleventh-century funerary complex at Tampaksiring, north-east of Ubud, where ten candi are cut in relief into seven-metre niches in the cliffs on both banks of the Pakerisan river. The shrines are understood to commemorate King Anak Wungsu of the Udayana line and his favoured queens, with the eastern group associated with King Udayana, Queen Mahendradatta and their sons. A legible inscription on the northern shrine reads Haji Lumahing Jalu, taken to mean that the king made a temple here.

name: Pura Ulun Danu Bratan
deity: Dewi Danu, goddess of lake and river; main meru to Shiva and Parvati
significance: A Shaivite water temple built in 1633 on the shore of Lake Bratan near Bedugul in central Bali, honouring Dewi Danu, goddess of the waters, with an eleven-tiered pelinggih meru dedicated to Shiva and Parvati and a Buddha image also enshrined. Laid out on a square plan with three courtyards behind decorated gates and thatched pagoda-roofed merus, it sits at the head of the irrigation system that supplies the region, linked to downstream temples belonging to each subak or irrigation society.
story: Because its shrines stand on small islets, the temple appears to float when the level of the lake rises, which is why it is popularly called the Bali temple on the lake.
